text: Defense in depth is a real, standard security principle: don't rely on one wall or one lock. Build several independent layers, each catching a different kind of failure, so one layer breaking doesn't mean the whole system is compromised. On the Now Platform, you've already built five such layers across this path, scattered across different courses, months apart. This lesson names all five together for the first time, so you see one coherent model instead of five separate topics.

An administrator asks whether one ACL is configured correctly — necessary, but not the whole job. A flawless ACL configuration alone does not make an instance secure, because ACLs are only one of five independent layers the platform actually relies on. An instance can have perfect ACLs and still be insecure if the other four layers are ignored.

Five layers, all covered already in this path. ACLs handle table and field access, from System Administration's ACL chapter. UI Policies and Data Policies split client-side from server-side enforcement, also from System Administration, echoed by Business Rules and Client Scripts in Scripting & Application Development. Application Scope isolation, from that same scripting course, keeps one custom app from reaching another's tables. MID Server network isolation, from IntegrationHub & REST APIs, lets the instance reach on-premises systems without opening an inbound firewall port. And authentication — this course's own Chapter Three — decides who gets to make a request at all.

Trace a single request through all five: authentication decides who you are, application scope decides whether your app can even reach the table, the ACL decides whether you specifically can touch this record and field, a UI or Data Policy validates the value itself, and if the request needs to reach an on-premises system, the MID Server carries it out through an outbound-only connection. Five independent checks, not one check wearing five names.

A security architect's real job is seeing this whole model at once: knowing which layer backs up which other layer, and recognizing that any layer with nothing backing it up has to be bulletproof, because nothing else will catch a mistake there. That's the real difference between administering security and architecting it.
